phy_edx.14.0.summary: To change the shape of an object (stretch, bend or compress it) you must apply **more than one force**, because a single force on its own would just make the whole object accelerate instead of distorting it. Distortion can be **elastic**, where the object returns to its original shape and size once the forces are removed, or **inelastic**, where it is permanently deformed and does not return to its original shape. Whether distortion is elastic depends on the material and on whether the **elastic limit** has been exceeded.

core.p: **Distortion** (also called deformation) is any change in the shape or size of an object caused by forces. At GCSE the three types you must name are **stretching**, **bending** and **compressing**. Squashing a sponge, bending a diving board and stretching a rubber band are all distortion.
bullets: **Stretching** (tension): forces pull outwards and the object gets longer.
**Compressing**: forces push inwards and the object gets shorter or squashed.
**Bending**: forces act so that one side of the object is stretched and the other side is compressed.
Distortion happens to every solid object to some extent; a stiff object just distorts by a tiny amount.
The change in length when an object is stretched is called its **extension**; when it is squashed it is a **compression**.

core.h: Why one force is not enough
core.p: This is the key idea of 15.1. If only **one force** acts on an object, there is a **resultant force**, so by Newton's second law the object **accelerates** in the direction of the force. It moves as a whole instead of changing shape. To stretch, bend or compress an object while it stays in place, you need **at least two forces** acting in different directions or at different points.
bullets: Pull one end of a spring lying on a smooth table and the whole spring just slides towards you; it does not stretch much.
To stretch it you must **hold the other end** (a second force) or fix it to a support.
A spring hanging from a clamp is stretched by **two** forces: the **weight** of the mass pulling down and the **support** pulling up.
When the object is stationary and distorted, the forces are **balanced** (resultant force = zero).
The forces must act at **different points** on the object, otherwise they could not change its shape.

callouts.p: Stretching, bending or compressing an object requires more than one force. With a single force the object would accelerate rather than change shape.
In explain questions, always name BOTH forces and say where they act, for example 'weight of the mass acting down on the bottom of the spring and the clamp pulling up on the top'.

core.p: To stretch something, two forces must pull on it in **opposite directions**, away from the middle of the object. The object gets longer; the increase in length is the **extension**.
bullets: Tug of war rope: each team pulls on one end, so the rope is in tension.
Hanging spring: weight acts down at the bottom, clamp force acts up at the top.
Rubber band stretched between two fingers: each finger pulls outwards.
Extension = stretched length - original length.
Larger pair of forces gives a bigger extension (until the elastic limit is reached).

callouts.p: Extension is NOT the total stretched length. Always subtract the original (natural) length.

core.p: To compress an object, two forces must **push inwards** towards each other on opposite ends. The object gets shorter. A spring that is compressed stores energy, just like a stretched one.
bullets: Squeezing a spring between finger and thumb: both push inwards.
Standing on a bathroom scale: your weight pushes down on the spring, the floor pushes up.
Car suspension springs are compressed between the car body and the axle.
Sitting on a cushion: your weight pushes down, the chair pushes up; the foam is squashed.
Compression = original length - compressed length.

core.p: Bending needs forces that are **not all along the same line**. A typical case is a ruler or plank supported at both ends with a load in the middle: that is **three forces**, two upward support forces and one downward push. When something bends, the **outer (convex) side is stretched** and the **inner (concave) side is compressed**.
bullets: Plank across two bricks with a person standing in the middle: 2 upward support forces + 1 downward weight.
Diving board: clamped at one end (support force and turning effect) with the diver's weight at the other end.
Bending a ruler with two hands: hands push in opposite directions at different points.
Because one side stretches and the other compresses, bending combines both types of distortion.
The forces are balanced when the bent object is stationary.

callouts.p: For a beam on two supports, say there are three forces: the load acting down in the middle and a reaction force from each support acting up.

core.p: An object is **elastically distorted** if it **returns to its original shape and size when the forces are removed**. All the energy transferred to the object while stretching it is stored as **elastic potential energy** and can be fully recovered.
bullets: Examples: a spring with a small mass, a rubber band, a trampoline bed, a bow string, a squash ball.
There is **no permanent change** in length or shape.
Elastic distortion happens as long as the **elastic limit** is not exceeded.
For many objects (e.g. springs) elastic distortion at small forces is also **proportional**: doubling the force doubles the extension (Hooke's law, covered in 15.3).
Elastic objects are useful when we want them to be reused: springs in pens, mattresses, suspension.

callouts.p: A change of shape where the object returns to its original shape and size when the deforming forces are removed.

core.p: An object is **inelastically distorted** if it **does not return to its original shape** when the forces are removed: it is **permanently deformed**. Some of the work done on it is not stored as elastic potential energy but is transferred to the thermal store and used to rearrange the particles permanently.
bullets: Examples: plasticine or modelling clay, a crushed drinks can, a car body panel after a crash, a spring stretched too far, chewing gum.
There is a **permanent extension** (or permanent change of shape).
Happens when an object is stretched **beyond its elastic limit**, or with materials like clay that are inelastic even at small forces.
Inelastic distortion is useful in car crumple zones: the metal deforms permanently, which increases the time of the collision and absorbs energy.
Sometimes called **plastic deformation**.

callouts.p: A change of shape where the object does not return to its original shape when the deforming forces are removed; it is permanently deformed.

core.p: The single test is: **remove the forces and see what happens**. If the object goes back to exactly its original shape and length, the distortion was elastic. If there is any permanent change, it was inelastic.
bullets: The same object can show both: a spring is elastic with small loads but inelastic if overloaded.
Use the phrase **'returns to its original shape (and length)'** for elastic.
Use the phrase **'permanently deformed / does not return to its original shape'** for inelastic.
Measuring the length after unloading is how you test this experimentally.
Energy: elastic means stored energy is recoverable; inelastic means some energy is dissipated.

core.p: The **elastic limit** is the point beyond which an object will **no longer return to its original shape** when the force is removed. Below it, distortion is elastic; above it, the object is permanently deformed.
bullets: Different materials and objects have different elastic limits.
A strong steel spring has a high elastic limit; a weak thin spring has a low one.
If you exceed the elastic limit and then unload, the object is longer than it was originally.
For springs, the **limit of proportionality** (where the force-extension graph stops being a straight line) is usually close to the elastic limit.
In practicals, use loads that stay below the elastic limit if you want to reuse the spring.

callouts.p: The maximum force (or extension) an object can have and still return to its original shape when the force is removed.
Do not say the spring 'breaks' at the elastic limit. Beyond the elastic limit it is permanently stretched; breaking happens much later.

core.h: What happens to the particles (grade 9 depth)
core.p: In a solid, particles are held in place by forces of attraction acting like tiny springs between them. When an object is stretched **elastically**, the particles are pulled slightly further apart but stay in the same arrangement, so when the force is removed the attraction pulls them back. When it is stretched **beyond the elastic limit**, layers of particles **slide past each other** into new positions, so they cannot return.
bullets: Elastic: bonds stretched, not broken or rearranged, so shape is restored.
Inelastic: particles move to new positions permanently.
This is why work done in inelastic stretching is partly dissipated as heat rather than stored.
Rubber is elastic because its long coiled molecules uncoil when stretched and recoil afterwards.
Plasticine is inelastic because its particles slide easily past each other even with small forces.

core.p: When forces distort an object, they **do work** on it, because each force moves its point of application. For elastic distortion this work is **stored in the elastic potential energy store** of the object and can be fully transferred back, for example when a stretched catapult fires a stone.
bullets: Elastic: work done = energy stored in the elastic potential energy store.
Inelastic: work done > energy stored, because some is dissipated (heating the material).
A trampoline or bungee cord transfers kinetic energy to the elastic store and back.
The equation E = 1/2 x k x x squared for energy stored only applies for elastic, linear stretching (covered in 15.4).

callouts.p: Energy stored in an elastically distorted object is recoverable; energy used in inelastic distortion is not all recoverable.

core.p: Engineers choose materials based on whether elastic or inelastic behaviour is wanted. Designs must keep everyday loads **well below the elastic limit** so parts are not permanently damaged.
bullets: Elastic wanted: springs, suspension, climbing ropes, trampolines, bungee cords, mattress springs.
Inelastic wanted: car crumple zones, cycle helmet foam liners (designed to crush once), modelling clay, shaping metal by pressing.
Bungee cords are tested so the jumper never takes them past the elastic limit.
A helmet or car that has been in a crash should be replaced because it has been permanently deformed.

analogy.t: A crowd of people holding hands
analogy.p: Imagine rows of people holding hands in a hall. If you gently pull the end of the line while someone holds the other end (two forces), everyone leans apart a little and, when you let go, they spring back to where they were: that is elastic distortion. Pull too hard and people let go and grab new hands in new places; when you stop, the crowd is in a new shape: that is going past the elastic limit, inelastic distortion. If nobody holds the other end, the whole crowd just walks towards you, which is why one force accelerates rather than distorts. It breaks down because real particles do not choose to let go, and bonds in metals are not individual hands; the forces between particles act in all directions at once.

terms.d: A change in the shape or size of an object caused by forces acting on it.
Another word for distortion: a change of shape caused by forces.
Distortion in which forces pull outwards and the object gets longer.
Distortion in which forces push inwards and the object gets shorter.
Distortion in which one side of an object is stretched and the other compressed, needing forces not all in line.
Distortion where the object returns to its original shape and size when the forces are removed.
Distortion where the object does not return to its original shape when the forces are removed; it is permanently deformed.
Another name for inelastic distortion.
The point beyond which an object is permanently deformed and will not return to its original shape.
The increase in length of an object when stretched: stretched length minus original length.
The decrease in length of an object when squashed: original length minus compressed length.
The extra length left in an object after the force is removed, when it has been stretched beyond its elastic limit.
The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object combined.
Energy stored in a stretched, compressed or bent elastic object.
The pulling force in a stretched object such as a spring, rope or string.

mistakes.w: You only need one force to stretch a spring.
mistakes.r: More than one force is needed; with one force the spring would accelerate. E.g. weight down and support force up.

mistakes.w: Elastic means the object stretches a lot.
mistakes.r: Elastic means the object returns to its original shape and size when the force is removed.

mistakes.w: Inelastic means it doesn't stretch.
mistakes.r: Inelastic means it does not return to its original shape; it is permanently deformed.

mistakes.w: Past the elastic limit the spring snaps.
mistakes.r: Past the elastic limit it is permanently stretched (has a permanent extension); it does not necessarily break.

mistakes.w: Extension is the length of the spring.
mistakes.r: Extension = stretched length - original length.

mistakes.w: A bent ruler has only one force on it, the push.
mistakes.r: Bending a supported ruler involves three forces: the push/load and a support force at each end.

mistakes.w: The forces on a stretched stationary spring are unbalanced.
mistakes.r: The forces are balanced (equal and opposite) so the resultant force is zero.

mistakes.w: Elastic objects lose energy when they spring back.
mistakes.r: In elastic distortion the energy stored in the elastic potential energy store is recovered when the object returns to its shape.

exam.q: State what is meant by elastic distortion.
model: The object returns to its original shape/length when the force is removed.
exam.tip: Use the words 'original shape' and 'force removed'.

exam.q: State what is meant by inelastic distortion.
model: The object does not return to its original shape when the force is removed / it is permanently deformed.
exam.tip: 'Permanently' is the key word.

exam.q: Explain why at least two forces are needed to stretch a spring.
model: With only one force there would be a resultant force so the spring would accelerate / move.
A second force in the opposite direction (e.g. from the support) is needed so the spring stays in place and changes shape.
exam.tip: Link one force to acceleration, then say what the second force does.

exam.q: A spring hangs from a clamp with a mass attached. Name the two forces that stretch the spring and give their directions.
model: Weight of the mass (pull of the mass) acting downwards on the bottom of the spring.
Force from the clamp/support acting upwards on the top of the spring.
exam.tip: Give a direction for each force.

exam.q: Give one example of an object that shows inelastic distortion.
model: Any of: plasticine, clay, crushed can, car body in a crash, spring stretched beyond its elastic limit.
exam.tip: Pick an obvious example; avoid rubber bands.

exam.q: A student hangs a load on a spring and then removes it. The spring is now 2 cm longer than at the start. Explain what has happened.
model: The spring has been stretched beyond its elastic limit.
So it has been inelastically/permanently deformed and does not return to its original length.
exam.tip: Mention elastic limit and permanent deformation.

exam.q: A plank rests on two bricks and a child stands in the middle. Describe the forces acting on the plank and how it is distorted.
model: Weight of the child acts downwards on the middle of the plank.
Each brick exerts an upward (support/normal) force on the end of the plank.
The plank bends; it needs more than one force so it does not just accelerate.
The lower surface is stretched and the upper surface is compressed.
exam.tip: Three forces for a beam on two supports.

exam.q: Describe how you could test whether a rubber band is distorted elastically by a given load.
model: Measure the original length of the rubber band with a ruler.
Hang the load on it, then remove the load.
Measure the length again: if it is the same as the original length the distortion was elastic (if longer, inelastic).
exam.tip: The test is always what happens after the load is removed.

exam.q: Explain why car crumple zones are designed to deform inelastically rather than elastically.
model: Inelastic deformation transfers/dissipates energy (to thermal store) rather than storing it.
So the car does not bounce back; energy is not returned to the passengers / the crash takes longer, reducing the force.
exam.tip: Link inelastic to energy not being returned.

exam.q: Compare the behaviour of a steel spring and a piece of modelling clay when forces are applied to them and then removed. Refer to elastic and inelastic distortion and the elastic limit in your answer.
model: Both need more than one force to distort them, e.g. pulled at both ends or squeezed between hands.
The steel spring distorts elastically for small forces.
When the forces are removed the spring returns to its original shape and length.
Energy stored in the spring's elastic store is recovered.
If the spring is stretched beyond its elastic limit it is permanently stretched / does not return to original length.
Modelling clay distorts inelastically even with small forces.
It stays in its new shape when the forces are removed / is permanently deformed.
Energy used to shape the clay is not recovered / is dissipated.
exam.tip: Structure: forces needed, spring below limit, spring above limit, clay.

worked.q: A spring has an original length of 6.0 cm. With a load it is 9.5 cm long. When the load is removed it returns to 6.0 cm. Calculate the extension with the load and state the type of distortion.
steps: After unloading, length = 6.0 cm = original length, so no permanent extension.
worked.ans: Extension = 3.5 cm; the distortion was elastic.

worked.q: The same spring is loaded with a much bigger weight and stretches to 15.0 cm. After unloading it is 7.2 cm long. Find the permanent extension and explain what this shows.
steps: Permanent extension = length after unloading - original length
A permanent extension means the spring did not return to its original length.
So the load took the spring beyond its elastic limit.
worked.ans: Permanent extension = 1.2 cm; the spring was inelastically distorted because its elastic limit was exceeded.

worked.q: Model answer: explain, using a squash ball being squeezed, why compressing an object needs more than one force.
steps: If you push the ball with one finger only, there is a resultant force on it.
So it accelerates away from your finger instead of squashing.
Squeezing between finger and thumb gives two forces pushing inwards from opposite sides.
These forces are balanced, so the ball stays still but its shape changes (it is compressed).
worked.ans: Two inward forces in opposite directions are needed so that the ball changes shape instead of accelerating.

phy_edx.14.1.summary: For a spring (and many elastic objects) the force applied is **directly proportional** to the extension, as long as the limit of proportionality is not exceeded: **F = k x**, where k is the **spring constant** in N/m. This is a **linear** relationship, shown by a straight line through the origin on a force-extension graph; beyond the limit of proportionality, or for materials like rubber, the relationship is **non-linear** and the graph curves. Stretching an elastic object transfers energy to its elastic potential energy store, and for linear stretching **E = 1/2 x k x x squared**, which equals the area under the force-extension graph.

core.p: When you stretch a spring, the **extension** increases as the force increases. For a spring, up to the **limit of proportionality**, the extension is **directly proportional** to the force: double the force and you double the extension. This is called **Hooke's law**.
bullets: Equation: **force exerted on a spring (N) = spring constant (N/m) x extension (m)**, F = k x.
Extension x is measured in **metres** in the equation, so convert cm or mm first.
Directly proportional means: straight-line graph that **passes through the origin**.
The same equation applies to **compression** (x is then the compression).
You must **recall** this equation; it is not on the equation sheet.

callouts.p: force exerted on a spring = spring constant x extension, F = k x
The extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied, provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.

core.p: The **extension** is the **increase in length** compared with the spring's original (natural, unloaded) length. It is NOT the total length of the stretched spring.
bullets: Extension = stretched length - original length.
Example: original length 4.0 cm, stretched length 7.0 cm, extension = 3.0 cm = 0.030 m.
A force-extension graph always starts at (0, 0) because with no force there is no extension.
A force-length graph would NOT pass through the origin; it starts at the original length.
Unit conversions: 1 cm = 0.01 m, 1 mm = 0.001 m.

callouts.p: Using the total length instead of the extension, or forgetting to convert cm to m, is the most common way to lose marks on F = k x questions.

core.p: The **spring constant** tells you how **stiff** a spring is: it is the force needed to produce an extension of 1 m (or, in practice, the force per metre of extension). A **larger k** means a **stiffer** spring that needs more force for the same extension.
bullets: k = F / x, unit N/m.
Stiff spring (high k): steep force-extension graph, small extension for a given force.
Weak/soft spring (low k): shallow graph, large extension for a given force.
k depends on the material, the thickness of the wire, the diameter of the coils and the number of coils.
On a force (y-axis) against extension (x-axis) graph, **gradient = k**.

callouts.p: The force per unit extension of a spring, k = F / x, measured in N/m. It is a measure of the stiffness of the spring.
Check the axes! If the graph is extension (y) against force (x), the gradient is 1/k, not k.

core.p: Rearrange the equation depending on what is asked. Always write the equation, substitute with units in SI, then give the answer with units.
bullets: F = k x to find the force.
k = F / x to find the spring constant.
x = F / k to find the extension.
Weight of a hanging mass: W = m g, with g = 10 N/kg, gives the force on the spring.

callouts.p: If a question gives a mass in grams hanging on a spring, convert to kg, then use W = m g to get the force before using F = k x.

core.p: A **linear** relationship between force and extension gives a **straight line** on a graph. If the straight line also passes through the **origin**, the quantities are **directly proportional**. For a spring obeying Hooke's law the relationship is both linear and proportional.
bullets: Equal increases in force give equal increases in extension.
Gradient is constant, so k is constant.
You can calculate the spring constant only in the linear region, using k = F / x or the gradient.
Linear elastic distortion is what F = k x and E = 1/2 k x squared describe.
Metal springs and metal wires behave linearly for small forces.

core.p: A **non-linear** relationship gives a **curved** force-extension graph. Equal increases in force do NOT give equal increases in extension. F = k x does not apply because k is not constant.
bullets: A spring stretched beyond its **limit of proportionality**: the graph curves (usually becomes less steep, so extension increases more per newton).
**Rubber bands** are non-linear for most of their stretch: the graph is curved from early on.
Polythene/plastic strips are non-linear and also often inelastic.
In non-linear regions you cannot quote a single spring constant.
You can still find the work done from the **area under the curve** (for example by counting squares).

head: Linear
Non-linear
rows: Not constant, F = k x not valid

callouts.p: Linear = straight-line graph, F proportional to x, constant k. Non-linear = curved graph, k not constant.

core.h: Limit of proportionality and elastic limit
core.p: The **limit of proportionality** is the point where the force-extension graph **stops being a straight line**. Beyond it, Hooke's law no longer applies. The **elastic limit** is the point beyond which the spring will not return to its original length. For a spring these two points are very close together, so it is usually assumed that going past one means going past the other.
bullets: Below limit of proportionality: linear, F = k x applies.
Beyond it: non-linear, extension increases faster for each extra newton.
Beyond elastic limit: spring is permanently deformed (inelastic distortion).
In exam graph questions, the limit of proportionality is where the line starts to curve.

callouts.p: The point beyond which force is no longer directly proportional to extension; the graph stops being a straight line.
A curved section does not mean the spring has snapped. It still stretches, just not proportionally.

core.h: Work done in stretching a spring
core.p: To stretch a spring you apply a force that moves through a distance, so you **do work** on it. If the spring is not stretched beyond its elastic limit, **all the work done is stored** in the spring's **elastic potential energy store**. This energy can be transferred back, e.g. into kinetic energy when a catapult is released.
bullets: Work done = energy transferred.
Elastic stretching: work done = energy stored as elastic potential energy.
If the elastic limit is exceeded, some of the work done is dissipated (heating) and is not stored.
The force is not constant while stretching (it grows from 0 to F), which is why the energy is NOT simply F x x.

core.h: Energy stored: E = 1/2 k x squared
core.p: For linear elastic stretching, the energy transferred in stretching a spring is **energy transferred in stretching (J) = 0.5 x spring constant (N/m) x (extension (m)) squared**, E = 1/2 x k x x squared. This equation is given on the equation sheet, but you must be able to use and rearrange it.
bullets: Square the extension FIRST, then multiply by k and by 0.5.
Doubling the extension makes the energy stored **four times** larger (because of the squared).
Extension must be in metres for the answer to be in joules.
Rearranged: x = square root of (2E / k); k = 2E / x squared.
Only valid in the **linear** region (up to the limit of proportionality).

callouts.p: energy transferred in stretching = 0.5 x spring constant x (extension) squared, E = 1/2 x k x x squared
Writing (0.5 x k x x) squared, or forgetting to square x. Only the extension is squared.

core.p: The **work done** in stretching (energy stored) equals the **area under the force-extension graph**. For a linear graph this area is a **triangle**: area = 1/2 x base x height = 1/2 x x x F. Since F = k x, this becomes 1/2 x k x x squared, so the two methods agree.
bullets: Linear section: area of triangle = 1/2 x F x x.
Non-linear section: estimate the area by **counting squares** and multiplying by the energy each square represents.
Energy per square = (force per square) x (extension per square, in m).
Use axes in N and m to get the area in J.

callouts.p: If asked for energy stored and you are given F and x but not k, use E = 1/2 x F x x (the triangle area).

core.h: Why the energy is 1/2 F x and not F x (grade 9)
core.p: Work done = force x distance only when the force is **constant**. When stretching a spring the force starts at **zero** and rises steadily to F. The **average force** is therefore 1/2 F, so work done = average force x extension = 1/2 F x. Substituting F = k x gives 1/2 k x squared.
bullets: Average force for a linearly increasing force = (0 + F) / 2.
This is exactly the triangle area under the graph.
It explains why energy depends on x squared: both the force and the distance increase with x.
Good for 'explain' questions linking graph area, work done and energy stored.

core.h: Springs in combination and real-life uses
core.p: Knowing k lets engineers choose springs for a job. Stiff springs are used where large forces must produce small movement; soft springs where small forces must produce noticeable movement.
bullets: Newton meters use a spring with a known k: the extension shows the force, and the scale is evenly spaced because the spring is linear.
Car suspension: stiff springs (large k) to support the car's weight.
Pen springs and trampolines store elastic potential energy and return it.
Bathroom scales use compression of springs to measure weight.

callouts.p: A newton meter has an evenly spaced scale because its spring obeys Hooke's law (linear relationship).

analogy.p: Think of a spring as a savings jar where every extra newton of pull adds the same extra centimetre of stretch, like each pound coin raising a stack by the same height: that is a linear relationship, and the spring constant is how many pounds you need per centimetre. The energy stored is like the total effort of lifting every coin onto the growing stack: early coins only go up a little, later ones go up a lot, so the total grows with the height squared. Past the limit of proportionality the stack starts to lean and each coin adds a different height, so the simple rule fails. The analogy breaks down because coins are separate lumps, while force and extension change smoothly, and a stack of coins does not spring back to release energy.

terms.d: Extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied, up to the limit of proportionality.
Increase in length of a spring: stretched length minus original length.
Force per unit extension, k = F / x, in N/m; a measure of stiffness.
Two quantities increase by the same factor; the graph is a straight line through the origin.
A relationship that gives a straight-line graph; equal changes in one quantity give equal changes in the other.
A relationship that gives a curved graph; the ratio F / x is not constant.
Point beyond which force is no longer directly proportional to extension.
Point beyond which a spring will not return to its original length when the force is removed.
Energy stored in a stretched or compressed elastic object.
Energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance.
Graph of force against extension; gradient = spring constant in the linear region and area = work done.
Change in y divided by change in x on a graph; equals k on a force-extension graph.
Unit of force.
Unit of energy and work done; 1 J = 1 N m.
How hard it is to stretch an object; a stiffer spring has a larger spring constant.

mistakes.w: Uses the stretched length as x in F = k x.
mistakes.r: x is the extension: stretched length minus original length.

mistakes.w: Uses extension in cm in F = k x with k in N/m.
mistakes.r: Convert the extension to metres before substituting.

mistakes.w: E = 0.5 x k x x (forgets to square).
mistakes.r: E = 0.5 x k x (extension) squared.

mistakes.w: Energy stored = F x x.
mistakes.r: Energy stored = 1/2 x F x x, because the force increases from zero; it is the triangle area.

mistakes.w: A curved force-extension graph means the spring has broken.
mistakes.r: It means the spring has gone past the limit of proportionality; the relationship is non-linear.

mistakes.w: Linear and proportional mean the same thing.
mistakes.r: Proportional = linear AND passes through the origin.

mistakes.w: A higher spring constant means the spring stretches more.
mistakes.r: A higher spring constant means a stiffer spring that stretches less for the same force.

mistakes.w: Gradient of an extension-force graph is k.
mistakes.r: Gradient of force (y) against extension (x) is k; extension against force gives 1/k.

mistakes.w: Doubling the extension doubles the energy stored.
mistakes.r: Energy is proportional to extension squared, so doubling x gives four times the energy.

exam.q: State the equation linking force, spring constant and extension.
model: force = spring constant x extension (F = k x).
exam.tip: Words or symbols both accepted; this one must be recalled.

exam.q: A spring has a spring constant of 25 N/m. Calculate the force needed to stretch it by 0.12 m.
exam.tip: Show substitution for the first mark.

exam.q: A force of 6.0 N stretches a spring by 4.0 cm. Calculate the spring constant.
model: Convert: 4.0 cm = 0.040 m
exam.tip: Unit conversion is often a separate mark.

exam.q: A spring with k = 80 N/m is stretched by 0.050 m. Calculate the energy stored in the spring.
model: E = 0.5 x 80 x 0.050 squared
exam.tip: Square the extension first: 0.050 squared = 0.0025.

exam.q: Describe the difference between a linear and a non-linear relationship between force and extension.
model: Linear: force-extension graph is a straight line / extension increases by equal amounts for equal increases in force.
Non-linear: graph is curved / equal increases in force do not give equal increases in extension.
exam.tip: Refer to graph shape for each.

exam.q: Explain how a force-extension graph can be used to find the spring constant of a spring.
model: Find the gradient of the straight-line (linear) part of the graph.
Gradient = change in force / change in extension = k (with extension in m).
exam.tip: Say 'linear part' to show you know k is only valid there.

exam.q: Explain why the energy stored in a stretched spring is not equal to F x x.
model: The force increases from zero to F as the spring is stretched / is not constant.
So the average force is F/2 and energy = 1/2 F x / area of triangle under graph.
exam.tip: Link to the triangle under the graph.

exam.q: A spring is stretched with energy 0.36 J stored. Its spring constant is 200 N/m. Calculate the extension.
model: 0.36 = 0.5 x 200 x x squared
exam.tip: Rearrange before taking the square root.

exam.q: A mass of 300 g hangs from a spring of spring constant 40 N/m. Calculate the extension of the spring in cm. (g = 10 N/kg)
model: x = 7.5 cm
exam.tip: Two-step: weight first, then Hooke's law.

exam.q: Compare the force-extension behaviour of a metal spring and a rubber band as the force on each is increased. Include the terms linear, non-linear and limit of proportionality and explain how the energy stored can be found in each case.
model: Spring: force-extension graph is a straight line through the origin at first.
So extension is directly proportional to force / linear / obeys Hooke's law.
Beyond the limit of proportionality the spring's graph curves / becomes non-linear.
Rubber band: graph is curved for most of its stretch / non-linear.
Spring (linear region): energy stored = 1/2 k x squared or 1/2 F x / triangle area.
Rubber band: energy found from area under the curve, e.g. by counting squares.
Spring constant can only be found from the linear region.
exam.tip: Cover both objects, graph shapes, and both energy methods.

worked.q: A spring is 5.0 cm long unloaded. A 4.0 N weight makes it 7.5 cm long. Calculate (a) the spring constant and (b) the energy stored.
steps: E = 0.5 x k x x squared = 0.5 x 160 x 0.025 squared

worked.q: A force-extension graph for a spring is a straight line from (0, 0) to (0.20 m, 10 N). Find the spring constant and the work done stretching it to 0.20 m from the graph.
steps: Gradient = change in F / change in x = 10 / 0.20 = 50 N/m, so k = 50 N/m
Work done = area of triangle = 0.5 x 0.20 x 10
Check with equation: 0.5 x 50 x 0.20 squared = 0.5 x 50 x 0.04 = 1.0 J
worked.ans: k = 50 N/m; work done = 1.0 J

worked.q: A spring stores 0.20 J when stretched by 0.040 m. How much energy does it store when stretched by 0.080 m (still in the linear region)?
steps: E is proportional to x squared.
Extension doubles, so x squared increases by 2 squared = 4.

phy_edx.14.2.summary: In this core practical you hang a spring from a clamp, add masses one at a time and measure the **extension** with a vertical metre rule. Plotting **force (weight) against extension** gives a straight line through the origin in the linear region, whose **gradient is the spring constant k**. The **area under the force-extension graph** gives the **work done** in stretching the spring, which equals the energy stored in its elastic potential energy store while the spring stays below its limit of proportionality.

core.p: The Edexcel core practical is to **investigate the extension and work done when applying forces to a spring**. You must be able to describe the method, process the results (calculate extension and force), plot and interpret a force-extension graph, and evaluate the method.
bullets: Find the relationship between force and extension.
Find the **spring constant** from the gradient of the linear part of the graph.
Find the **work done** (energy stored) from the area under the graph.
Identify the **limit of proportionality** if the graph curves.
Exam questions often give a set of results and ask you to finish the table, plot the graph or spot an anomaly.

callouts.p: Independent variable: force (weight of masses). Dependent variable: extension. Control variable: same spring throughout (same material, coil size, temperature).

core.p: Everything must be set up so that the spring hangs freely and its length can be read accurately against a fixed vertical scale.
bullets: **Clamp stand** with two bosses and clamps (one for the spring, one for the ruler).
**Spring** hung from a clamp or hook.
**Metre rule**, clamped **vertically** next to the spring, with zero at the top.
**Mass hanger** (usually 100 g = 1 N) and slotted masses (100 g each).
**Pointer** (e.g. a splint or pin taped to the bottom of the spring) to read the scale precisely.
**G-clamp** or heavy weight to hold the clamp stand to the bench so it cannot topple.
Safety goggles.

core.p: Follow these steps in order. In a 6 mark method question, you should mention the setup, how you measure the original length, how you add the force, how you measure the new length and how you calculate extension.
bullets: Set up the clamp stand, clamp it to the bench, and hang the spring from the clamp.
Clamp the metre rule **vertically** beside the spring (check with a set square if needed).
Attach a pointer to the bottom of the spring and record the **original (unloaded) length / pointer position**.
Hang the mass hanger on the spring (adds 1 N). Wait for the spring to stop moving.
Read the new pointer position with your **eye level with the pointer** and record it.
Add masses in equal steps (e.g. 100 g at a time) and record the pointer position each time, up to at least 6 readings.
Calculate **extension = new length - original length** for each force.
Calculate **force = weight = mass (kg) x 10 N/kg**.
(Optional) Remove the masses one at a time and record the lengths again to check the spring returns (has not passed its elastic limit).

callouts.p: Always say 'measure the original length first' and 'extension = new length minus original length'. These are separate mark scheme points.

core.p: Being able to name the variables is a common 1 or 2 mark question.
bullets: **Independent variable**: the force applied (weight of the masses).
**Dependent variable**: the extension of the spring.
**Control variables**: the same spring each time, the same scale/ruler, same temperature.
The extension is calculated, not read directly: you measure lengths (or pointer positions).
To compare springs, the spring itself would become the independent variable, with the force range kept the same.

head: Variable type
In this practical
How it is controlled or measured
rows: Add 100 g (1 N) masses in equal steps
Metre rule and pointer, subtract original length
Do not swap springs or overstretch it

core.p: The main sources of error are **reading the ruler from an angle** (parallax), the spring still **oscillating**, and the ruler **not being vertical**.
bullets: Read the scale with your **eye level with the pointer** to avoid parallax error.
Use a **pointer** fixed to the bottom of the spring rather than guessing where the end is.
Wait for the spring to be **stationary** before reading.
Use a **set square** to check the ruler is vertical.
Repeat the readings (loading and unloading) and calculate a mean to reduce random error.
Use more, smaller mass steps to get more points and a more reliable line.

callouts.p: 'Repeat to make it more accurate' is vague. Say 'repeat and calculate a mean to reduce the effect of random errors' or 'read at eye level to avoid parallax error'.

core.p: The main hazards are **masses falling** onto feet and the **spring snapping or flying back** if overloaded.
bullets: Wear **safety goggles** in case the spring snaps or springs back.
**Clamp the stand to the bench** (G-clamp or counterweight) so it cannot topple.
Do not overload the spring; stop adding masses if it stretches a lot or stops returning.
Keep feet away from under the masses; you can place a tray or soft mat under them.
Stand up while working so you can move out of the way.

callouts.p: Always pair a hazard with its control measure: 'masses could fall on feet, so place a cushion underneath and keep feet clear'.

core.p: Results go in a table with columns for mass, force, pointer reading (length) and extension. Original length here = 20.0 cm.
bullets: Force (N) = mass (kg) x 10 N/kg.
Extension (cm) = length - 20.0 cm.
Equal force steps give roughly equal extension steps in the linear region.
Look for an **anomalous result**: one that does not fit the pattern; check it and repeat or leave it out of the line.
Convert extension to metres before calculating k in N/m.

core.p: Plot **force on the y-axis** and **extension on the x-axis** so that the gradient is k. Draw a straight **line of best fit** through the linear points; if the last points curve away, draw a smooth curve there.
bullets: Use a sensible scale that fills more than half the grid.
Label axes with quantity and unit: force / N, extension / m (or cm).
Plot points accurately with small crosses.
Line of best fit should pass through (0, 0) for a spring obeying Hooke's law.
In the sample data the last point (6.0 N, 15.6 cm) lies off the line: the spring has passed its limit of proportionality.

core.h: Finding the spring constant from the graph
core.p: In the linear region, **k = gradient = change in force / change in extension**. Use a large triangle on the straight line, and make sure extension is in **metres**.
bullets: From the sample data: 5.0 N gives 12.5 cm = 0.125 m.
Use points on the line of best fit, not individual data points, for the gradient.
Only use the straight part; beyond the limit of proportionality F = k x does not apply.
A steeper graph means a stiffer spring with a larger k.

callouts.p: Using extension in cm gives k in N/cm (here 0.40 N/cm) which is 100 times too small if you write N/m.

core.h: Finding the work done from the graph
core.p: The **work done** in stretching the spring equals the **area under the force-extension graph**. In the linear region this is a triangle: work done = 1/2 x force x extension. This equals the energy stored, 1/2 k x squared.
bullets: Sample: stretching to 0.125 m with 5.0 N: work done = 0.5 x 5.0 x 0.125 = 0.3125 J (about 0.31 J).
Check: 0.5 x 40 x 0.125 squared = 0.3125 J.
For a curved part, estimate the area by counting squares: number of squares x energy per square.
Energy per square = force per square (N) x extension per square (m).
Work done is in joules only if force is in N and extension in m.

core.p: You may be asked to suggest improvements or explain anomalies. Think about random errors (scattered readings) and systematic errors (all readings shifted).
bullets: Parallax error: improved by eye level reading and a pointer.
Zero error: forgetting the original length gives a systematic error; the graph would not pass through the origin.
Spring oscillating: wait until it is still.
Overloading: going beyond the elastic limit permanently changes the spring, so later repeats are invalid.
Unloading check: if the lengths on unloading differ from loading, the elastic limit has been exceeded.
Resolution: a metre rule reads to 1 mm; for small extensions use smaller masses steps or a stiffer scale with finer divisions.

callouts.p: If a graph of force against length (not extension) is drawn, it is a straight line with an intercept on the length axis equal to the original length.

core.p: A typical conclusion: **the extension of the spring is directly proportional to the force applied up to the limit of proportionality**, so the spring obeys Hooke's law, with spring constant equal to the gradient. Beyond that point the relationship becomes **non-linear**.
bullets: Quote evidence: straight line through the origin.
Give the value of k with unit N/m.
State the work done from the area with unit J.
Mention where the graph stops being linear if your data shows it.

analogy.p: Adding 100 g masses is like climbing a ladder with evenly spaced rungs: each mass is one rung of force, and for a Hooke's law spring each rung lowers the pointer by the same amount, so the readings make an even staircase that becomes a straight line on the graph. The work done is like the total effort of climbing, which grows faster the higher you go, giving the triangle area. When the rungs start to get further apart (bigger extension per mass), you have passed the limit of proportionality. It breaks down because a real spring stretches smoothly, not in jumps, and climbing effort comes from you, while here the energy is stored in the spring.

phy_edx.14.3.summary: A **fluid** (a liquid or a gas) exerts pressure because its moving particles collide with surfaces, and this pressure always produces a **force at right angles (normal) to any surface** it touches. The Earth's **atmosphere** is a relatively thin layer of air held around the Earth by gravity; the weight of the air above any surface causes **atmospheric pressure**, about 100 000 Pa at sea level. Atmospheric pressure **decreases with height** because there is less air above you, so less weight of air pressing down, and the air is also less dense with fewer particle collisions.

core.p: A **fluid** is any substance that can **flow**: all **liquids** and all **gases**. Their particles are free to move past each other, so a fluid takes the shape of its container and pushes on every part of the container it touches.
bullets: Liquids: particles close together but moving randomly past each other.
Gases: particles far apart, moving quickly and randomly in all directions.
Air, water, oil and blood are all fluids.
Solids are NOT fluids because their particles are fixed in place.
This topic is **triple (Physics) only**.

Fluid?

callouts.p: A liquid or a gas: a substance that can flow.

core.p: **Pressure** is the force acting **normal (at right angles) to a surface** per unit area of that surface. It is measured in **pascals (Pa)**, where 1 Pa = 1 N/m squared. A large force on a small area gives a large pressure.
bullets: Unit: pascal, Pa; 1 Pa = 1 N/m squared.
1 kPa = 1000 Pa.
Pressure in fluids is caused by particle collisions with surfaces.
The size of the force from a fluid on a surface depends on the pressure and on the area of the surface.
Calculations using pressure = force / area are covered in 15.10-15.11.

core.h: Why fluids exert pressure: particle model
core.p: Fluid particles move **randomly** at high speed. When a particle hits a surface it **changes momentum** and so exerts a small **force** on the surface. Billions of collisions every second add up to a steady force spread over the surface: that is the pressure.
bullets: Each collision pushes on the surface.
More collisions per second means more pressure.
Faster particles (higher temperature) collide harder and more often, so more pressure.
More particles in the same volume (higher density) means more collisions, so more pressure.
Because the particles move in all directions, a fluid pushes on surfaces in **all directions**.

callouts.p: Pressure in a gas is due to particles colliding with the surface; each collision produces a force on the surface.

core.h: Pressure acts normal to any surface
core.p: A key spec statement is that **pressure in fluids causes a force normal (at 90 degrees) to any surface**. Whatever the orientation of a surface, top, bottom, sides or a sloping face, the fluid pushes straight at it, perpendicular to it.
bullets: **Normal** means at right angles to the surface.
Water in a bottle with holes in the side: jets come out **at right angles** to the wall at first.
A diver or submarine is pushed on from all sides, inwards, at right angles to its surface.
Air pushes on the top, bottom and sides of objects equally at the same height.
Any sideways part of the particle impacts cancels out on average, leaving only the perpendicular push.

callouts.p: Pressure in fluids causes a force normal to any surface.
Do not say fluid pressure only pushes downwards. It acts in all directions, at right angles to every surface it touches.

core.h: A simple model of the Earth's atmosphere
core.p: The **atmosphere** is a layer of air (mainly nitrogen and oxygen) surrounding the Earth, held in place by the Earth's **gravity**. Compared with the size of the Earth it is **very thin**: most of the air is within about 10 km of the surface, while the Earth's radius is about 6400 km.
bullets: Air particles are attracted to the Earth by gravity, so the air has **weight**.
The air is **densest near the surface** because the air above compresses the air below.
With increasing height the air becomes **less dense** (thinner) and eventually fades into space; there is no sharp edge.
Air particles move randomly, colliding with each other and with surfaces.
The model treats the atmosphere as layers of air, each pressing down on the layers beneath.

callouts.p: The atmosphere is a thin layer of air around the Earth that gets less dense with increasing height.

core.p: **Atmospheric pressure** is the pressure exerted by the air on any surface. You can think of it in two linked ways: (1) the **weight of the column of air above** a surface pressing on it, and (2) the **collisions of air particles** with the surface. Both explanations are accepted and they describe the same thing.
bullets: At sea level atmospheric pressure is about **100 000 Pa** (100 kPa, roughly 101 kPa).
That is like the weight of about 10 tonnes of air pressing on every square metre.
We are not crushed because the fluids inside our bodies push outwards with a similar pressure.
Atmospheric pressure acts in **all directions**, normal to every surface, not just downwards.
A barometer measures atmospheric pressure.

callouts.p: The pressure caused by the weight of the air above a surface (or by collisions of air particles with the surface); about 100 000 Pa at sea level.

core.h: Why atmospheric pressure decreases with height
core.p: As you go **higher**, atmospheric pressure **decreases**. This is a favourite explain question and needs two linked ideas: **less air above you** and **air becoming less dense**.
bullets: At greater height there is a **smaller column of air above** the surface.
So the **weight of air above** pressing down is **smaller**, giving lower pressure.
The air is also **less dense** at height (fewer particles per cubic metre) because less air above is compressing it.
Fewer particles per unit volume means **fewer collisions per second** with a surface, so less force per unit area.
The pressure does not fall in a straight line: it falls quickly at first and then more slowly, because density also falls.

callouts.p: For full marks link: higher up -> less air above -> smaller weight of air -> lower pressure. Add: air less dense -> fewer collisions per second.

core.h: Evidence of atmospheric pressure in everyday life
core.p: Because atmospheric pressure is large and acts in all directions, removing air from one side of a surface produces large forces.
bullets: **Crushed can demonstration**: boil a little water in a can, seal or invert it in cold water; the steam condenses, pressure inside drops and the outside air pressure crushes the can.
**Suction cups** stick because air pressure outside pushes them against the surface when air is squeezed out from underneath.
**Drinking through a straw**: you lower the pressure in your mouth and atmospheric pressure pushes the drink up.
Ears 'pop' in planes or lifts because the outside pressure changes with height while the pressure inside your ear lags behind.
A sealed crisp packet taken up a mountain swells because the outside pressure falls.

callouts.p: 'Suction' does not pull anything. It is the higher atmospheric pressure outside that pushes.

core.h: Forces on a surface from atmospheric pressure
core.p: The **force** from a fluid on a surface depends on the **pressure** and the **area**. Because atmospheric pressure is about 100 000 Pa, even a small area experiences a large force, which is normally balanced by an equal pressure on the other side.
bullets: A window of area 1 m squared has about 100 000 N pushing on each side; they cancel, so the window does not move.
If the pressure on one side is reduced, there is a resultant force towards the low pressure side.
Aircraft cabins are pressurised: the higher pressure inside pushes outwards on the walls at altitude, so the fuselage must be strong.
The force is always normal to the surface.

core.h: Pressure in liquids compared with gases
core.p: Liquids also exert pressure normal to surfaces and it increases with depth, just as air pressure increases as you go down through the atmosphere. The main difference is that liquids are almost **incompressible**, so their density is nearly the same at all depths, whereas air is **compressible** and gets denser lower down.
bullets: Gas: density changes a lot with height, so pressure does not change uniformly.
Liquid: density almost constant, so pressure increases steadily with depth (details in 15.12-15.14).
Both: pressure acts in all directions, normal to surfaces.
Both: deeper in the fluid means more fluid above, so more weight pressing down.

core.p: The particle model also explains why the pressure of a gas changes with temperature. This helps you explain pressure in fluids in terms of particles at grade 9 level.
bullets: Heating a gas increases the average kinetic energy of its particles.
Particles hit surfaces faster and more often.
So the force on the surface, and the pressure, increase (if the volume is fixed).
Weather: regions of high and low atmospheric pressure are partly caused by differences in air temperature.

callouts.p: More collisions per second, or harder collisions, give a larger pressure.

analogy.p: Imagine a tall stack of soft mattresses. The bottom mattress is squashed flat by the weight of all those above it, while the top one is barely squashed at all. The atmosphere is like this: the air at the bottom is squashed (dense) by the weight of the air above, so the pressure is largest at the ground, and higher up there is less above, so less squashing and lower pressure. The analogy breaks down because mattresses only push downwards on the one below, while air particles move randomly and push in all directions on every surface, and air has no layers or clear top.

terms.d: A liquid or a gas; a substance that can flow.

mistakes.w: Fluid pressure only acts downwards.
mistakes.r: Pressure in a fluid acts in all directions and causes a force normal to any surface.

mistakes.w: Pressure decreases with height because it is colder.
mistakes.r: There is less air above, so a smaller weight of air; and air is less dense, so fewer particle collisions.

mistakes.w: There is less gravity higher up so pressure falls.
mistakes.r: Gravity changes very little at these heights; the key reason is less air (weight) above and lower density.

mistakes.w: Fluids push on surfaces at any angle.
mistakes.r: The force due to fluid pressure is always normal (at right angles) to the surface.

mistakes.w: A suction cup is pulled onto the wall.
mistakes.r: Atmospheric pressure outside pushes it onto the wall because the pressure underneath is lower.

mistakes.w: The atmosphere is very thick compared with the Earth.
mistakes.r: It is a relatively thin layer; most air is within about 10 km of the surface.

mistakes.w: Air particles at the top of the atmosphere are closer together.
mistakes.r: Air is less dense higher up: particles are further apart.

mistakes.w: Pressure is caused by particles colliding with each other.
mistakes.r: Pressure on a surface is caused by particles colliding with that surface.

exam.q: State the direction of the force produced by a fluid's pressure on a surface.
model: Normal / at right angles / perpendicular to the surface.
exam.tip: Use the word normal or perpendicular.

exam.q: State what is meant by a fluid.
model: A liquid or a gas / a substance that can flow.
exam.tip: Give both liquid and gas.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of particles, how a gas exerts a pressure on the walls of its container.
model: Gas particles move randomly and collide with the walls.
Each collision exerts a force on the wall; force per unit area is pressure.
exam.tip: Collisions with the walls, then force.

exam.q: Describe a simple model of the Earth's atmosphere.
model: A (relatively thin) layer of air / gas around the Earth held by gravity.
That becomes less dense with increasing height.
exam.tip: Thin layer + density falls with height.

exam.q: Give the approximate value of atmospheric pressure at sea level.
model: About 100 000 Pa / 100 kPa (accept 101 kPa).
exam.tip: Include the unit.

exam.q: Explain why atmospheric pressure decreases with increasing height above the Earth's surface.
model: At greater height there is less air above / a shorter column of air.
So the weight of air above is smaller.
Air is less dense so there are fewer particle collisions (per second) with a surface.
exam.tip: Two separate ideas: weight of air above and density.

exam.q: A sealed bag of crisps is taken from sea level to the top of a mountain. Explain why the bag swells.
model: Atmospheric pressure outside the bag is lower at the top of the mountain.
Pressure of gas inside is now greater than outside, so there is a resultant outward force on the bag.
exam.tip: Compare inside and outside pressure.

exam.q: Water is put in a plastic bottle with three holes in its side. Describe and explain the direction of the water as it leaves each hole.
model: The water comes out at right angles to the side of the bottle (before curving down).
Because pressure in a fluid causes a force normal to the surface.
exam.tip: Link observation to the spec statement.

exam.q: Explain why a can containing a little boiling water collapses when it is sealed and cooled.
model: Steam inside condenses as it cools, so there are fewer gas particles inside / the pressure inside falls.
Atmospheric pressure outside is now greater than the pressure inside.
So there is a resultant inward force on the can which crushes it.
exam.tip: Pressure difference causes the resultant force.

exam.q: Explain how the atmosphere produces a pressure on the Earth's surface and why the pressure is different at the bottom and top of a mountain. Use ideas about particles and the weight of air.
model: The atmosphere is a layer of air held around the Earth by gravity, so the air has weight.
The weight of the column of air above a surface pushes on it, producing pressure.
Air particles move randomly and collide with the surface; each collision exerts a force.
Pressure acts in all directions / normal to the surface.
At the top of the mountain there is less air above, so less weight of air and lower pressure.
Air is less dense at the top (fewer particles per unit volume) because less air is compressing it.
So there are fewer collisions per second with a surface, giving lower pressure.
exam.tip: Structure: model, cause, particles, then compare heights using both weight and density.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why a diver feels water pushing on her from all sides, including from below.
steps: Water is a fluid; its particles move randomly in all directions.
Particles collide with every part of the diver's body.
So the water exerts a pressure that causes a force normal to every surface of her body.
This means forces act inwards on her from above, below and the sides.
worked.ans: Pressure in a fluid causes a force normal to any surface, so it acts on her from all directions.

worked.q: Atmospheric pressure is 100 000 Pa. Using the data table, by how much does it drop between sea level and the top of Mount Everest, and what fraction remains?
steps: Pressure at sea level = 100 kPa; at Everest = 33 kPa.
This is why climbers carry oxygen: the air is much less dense with fewer particles per breath.
worked.ans: Drop of about 67 000 Pa; about one third of sea-level pressure remains.

worked.q: Model answer: Why does an aircraft cabin need to be strong when flying at 11 km?
steps: The cabin is pressurised to near ground-level pressure (about 75-100 kPa).
Outside atmospheric pressure at 11 km is much lower (about 23 kPa), because there is less air above.
The pressure inside is greater than outside, so there is a resultant force outwards, normal to every part of the cabin wall.
Over the large area of the fuselage this force is huge, so the walls must be strong.
worked.ans: The pressure difference between inside and outside produces a large outward force normal to the cabin walls.

phy_edx.14.4.summary: Pressure tells you how concentrated a force is: it is the **force acting normal (at right angles) to a surface divided by the area of that surface**, P = F / A, measured in **pascals (Pa)**, where 1 Pa = 1 N/m². The same force spread over a large area gives a low pressure (snowshoes, tractor tyres), while the same force on a tiny area gives a huge pressure (drawing pins, knives). Grade 9 answers explain examples by saying which quantity (force or area) changes and what that does to the pressure, and handle unit conversions such as cm² to m² confidently.

core.p: Pressure is a measure of how much force acts on each unit of area of a surface. It is not the same thing as force: two objects can push with exactly the same force but produce very different pressures if the areas in contact are different.
bullets: Pressure = **force normal to a surface / area of that surface**.
Only the component of force acting **at right angles (normal)** to the surface counts.
Pressure is a **scalar**: it has size but no direction of its own; the force it produces on a surface acts normal to that surface.
Bigger force on the same area means **bigger pressure** (P is directly proportional to F).
Same force on a bigger area means **smaller pressure** (P is inversely proportional to A).

callouts.p: The force acting normal (at right angles) to a surface per unit area of that surface.

core.p: You must recall this equation for the exam; it is not always given on the equation sheet, so learn it and its rearrangements.
bullets: **pressure (Pa) = force normal to a surface (N) / area of that surface (m²)**
Symbols: **P = F / A**
Rearranged for force: **F = P × A**
Rearranged for area: **A = F / P**
Use the formula triangle with F on top and P and A underneath if it helps you rearrange.

callouts.p: P = F / A with P in Pa, F in N and A in m².

core.p: The SI unit of pressure is the pascal. One pascal is a very small pressure (roughly a sheet of paper resting on a table), so you will often see kilopascals and sometimes N/cm².
bullets: If area is in cm² and force in N, the answer is in **N/cm²**, not Pa.
**1 N/cm² = 10 000 Pa**, because 1 m² = 10 000 cm².
Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about **100 000 Pa (100 kPa)**.

callouts.p: 1 m = 100 cm but 1 m² = 100 × 100 = 10 000 cm². To change cm² to m², divide by 10 000, not by 100.

core.p: When a force is spread over a large area, each small piece of the surface carries only a small share of it, so the pressure is low and the surface is less likely to be damaged or to sink. When the same force is concentrated onto a tiny area, each bit of surface carries a large share, so the pressure is high and the object can cut or pierce the surface.
bullets: Halve the area with the same force: **pressure doubles**.
Double the area with the same force: **pressure halves**.
Double the force on the same area: **pressure doubles**.
A surface such as snow, mud or skin gives way when the pressure on it exceeds what it can withstand, not simply when the force is large.

callouts.p: Always name the quantity that changes (area), say which way (larger), and link it to pressure (smaller), e.g. 'larger area so smaller pressure for the same weight'.

fig.cap: The same brick (same weight, 20 N) gives a lower pressure when lying flat on a large face than when standing on its small end, because the force is spread over a bigger area.

core.h: Examples where a large area gives low pressure
core.p: Engineers and nature both increase area when they want to reduce pressure and stop something sinking in or causing damage.
bullets: **Snowshoes and skis**: spread the person's weight over a large area so the pressure on the snow is low and they do not sink.
**Wide tractor and tank tyres / caterpillar tracks**: low pressure on soft ground so the vehicle does not sink into mud.
**Camel's wide feet**: spread weight over sand.
**Foundations of buildings**: wide footings spread the building's weight so the ground underneath is not overloaded.
**Rucksack and bag straps that are wide**: lower pressure on the shoulders, so more comfortable.
**Lying flat on thin ice** to reach someone: larger area, lower pressure, so the ice is less likely to break.

core.h: Examples where a small area gives high pressure
core.p: When you want to cut, pierce or push into something, you make the contact area as small as possible so a modest force gives a very large pressure.
bullets: **Drawing pin**: the force from your thumb acts on the wide head (low pressure on thumb) but the same force acts on the tiny point (very high pressure, pierces the board).
**Sharp knife**: the thin edge has a tiny area, so the pressure is high enough to cut.
**Needles and nails**: tiny tip area.
**Stiletto heels** can damage floors, because the whole weight acts on a very small heel area.
**Ice skates**: thin blade gives a high pressure on the ice.

callouts.p: The force is the same at both ends of the pin; only the area differs, so the pressure on the board is much greater than on the thumb.

core.p: The equation uses the force acting at right angles to the surface. For an object resting on horizontal ground, that normal force is simply its weight. If a force pushes at an angle, only the part acting perpendicular to the surface creates pressure on it.
bullets: Object on horizontal floor: **F = weight = mass × gravitational field strength (W = m × g)**.
Take **g = 10 N/kg** on Earth unless told otherwise.
Forces that slide along a surface (parallel to it) do not add to the pressure on it.
If a question gives you a mass, convert it to weight first.

callouts.p: Never put a mass in kg straight into P = F / A. Work out the weight in newtons first using W = m × g.

core.p: Many questions ask you to work out the area first. Use the right shape formula and remember to count every contact point, such as four table legs or two feet.
bullets: Rectangle: **area = length × width**.
Circle: **area = π × r²** (r is the radius, half the diameter).
Several identical contacts: **total area = number of contacts × area of one**.
Standing on one foot halves the area compared with two feet, so the pressure doubles.
Convert lengths to metres before multiplying if you want the answer in Pa.

Change

rows: Person stands on one foot instead of two

core.p: Because P = F / A, pressure is directly proportional to force (area constant) and inversely proportional to area (force constant). Using ratios saves time and is often tested in multiple choice.
bullets: F × 3 with A fixed: P × 3.
A × 4 with F fixed: P ÷ 4.
F × 2 and A × 2 together: **P unchanged**.
A graph of P against A (fixed F) is a curve falling towards zero; P against 1/A is a straight line through the origin.

core.h: Pressure on any surface acts at right angles
core.p: A pressure on a surface always produces a force normal to that surface. This links P = F / A to the next spec points on fluids, where the pressure of a liquid or gas pushes at right angles on every surface it touches.
bullets: Force from pressure on a surface: **F = P × A**, acting at 90° to the surface.
A large area exposed to a pressure difference gets a large force, e.g. air pressure on a window during a storm.
This is why hydraulic machines can multiply force: the same pressure acting on a bigger piston area gives a bigger force (F = P × A).

callouts.p: If a question gives pressure and area and asks for force, rearrange to F = P × A, and check area is in m² if P is in Pa.

core.p: Edexcel calculation questions reward a clear method, so lay your working out in the same order every time.
bullets: 1. Write the equation: **P = F / A**.
2. Convert units: mass to weight (W = m × g), cm² or mm² to m², kPa to Pa.
3. Rearrange if needed before substituting.
4. Substitute the numbers with units.
5. Give the answer with the correct unit (Pa or N/m²) and sensible significant figures.

callouts.p: Even if your final answer is wrong, marks are given for the correct substitution, so always write the numbers into the equation.

analogy.p: Imagine 20 people standing on a giant trampoline. If they spread out over the whole surface, each square metre carries only a little weight and the mat barely dips (low pressure). If all 20 squeeze onto one small patch, that patch carries all the weight and the mat stretches deeply or tears (high pressure). The total weight (force) is the same in both cases; only how concentrated it is (force per area) changes. It breaks down because people are separate lumps, whereas a real force is spread smoothly over its contact area, and because the trampoline stretching is not what defines pressure: pressure exists even when the surface does not deform at all.

terms.d: Force acting normal to a surface per unit area of that surface; P = F / A.
A push or pull on an object, measured in newtons (N).
A force acting at right angles (perpendicular) to a surface.
The size of a surface, measured in square metres (m²).
The SI unit of pressure; 1 Pa is a force of 1 N acting on an area of 1 m².
Unit of pressure identical to the pascal.
1000 pascals.
The gravitational force on an object; W = m × g, measured in N.
Force per unit mass due to gravity; about 10 N/kg on Earth.
When one quantity doubles the other doubles; pressure and force at constant area.
When one quantity doubles the other halves; pressure and area at constant force.
The area of the surfaces actually touching, over which the force is spread.
A quantity with magnitude only and no direction; pressure is a scalar.
At 90 degrees to a line or surface.

mistakes.w: Pressure is the force on an object.
mistakes.r: Pressure is the force normal to a surface per unit area (force divided by area).

mistakes.w: Snowshoes reduce the force on the snow.
mistakes.r: The force (weight) is the same; snowshoes increase the area, so the pressure is smaller.

mistakes.w: Putting mass in kg straight into P = F / A.
mistakes.r: Calculate weight first: W = m × g, then divide by area.

mistakes.w: Converting cm² to m² by dividing by 100.
mistakes.r: 1 m² = 10 000 cm², so divide by 10 000.

mistakes.w: Writing the unit of pressure as N or N/m.
mistakes.r: Pa or N/m².

mistakes.w: Using P = F × A.
mistakes.r: P = F / A; F = P × A is the rearrangement for force.

mistakes.w: The drawing pin point has a bigger force than the head.
mistakes.r: The force is the same at both ends; the point has a much smaller area so a much bigger pressure.

mistakes.w: Using the area of one table leg when the table has four.
mistakes.r: Total contact area = 4 × area of one leg.

mistakes.w: A sharp knife cuts because it is pushed harder.
mistakes.r: A sharp knife has a smaller area of edge, so the same force gives a greater pressure.

exam.q: State the equation linking pressure, force normal to a surface and area of that surface.
model: pressure = force normal to a surface / area of that surface (P = F / A)
exam.tip: Write it in words or standard symbols; do not use a triangle as your only answer.

exam.q: State the unit of pressure.
model: pascal (Pa) or N/m²
exam.tip: N/m² is accepted; N/m is not.

exam.q: A box exerts a force of 600 N on the floor over an area of 0.3 m². Calculate the pressure on the floor.
exam.tip: Include the unit for the final mark.

exam.q: Explain why a camel with wide feet does not sink into soft sand.
model: wide feet give a large (contact) area
so the pressure on the sand is smaller for the same weight
exam.tip: Link area to pressure; do not say the force is smaller.

exam.q: A pressure of 50 000 Pa acts on a piston of area 0.02 m². Calculate the force on the piston.
model: F = P × A
exam.tip: Rearrange before substituting.

exam.q: A student of weight 500 N stands on one foot. The area of the foot in contact with the ground is 250 cm². Calculate the pressure in Pa.
exam.tip: The conversion of cm² to m² is usually worth its own mark.

exam.q: Explain why a drawing pin can be pushed into a board easily but does not hurt the thumb.
model: the force on the thumb and on the board is the same
the head has a large area so the pressure on the thumb is low
the point has a very small area so the pressure on the board is very high
exam.tip: Use the phrase 'same force' to show you understand only area changes.

exam.q: A crate of mass 120 kg rests on a floor on a base measuring 0.40 m by 0.50 m. g = 10 N/kg. Calculate the pressure on the floor.
exam.tip: Two steps before the pressure equation: weight and area.

exam.q: A pressure of 4 kPa acts on a surface. What area is needed for this pressure to produce a force of 800 N?
model: 4 kPa = 4000 Pa
A = 0.2 m²
exam.tip: Convert kPa to Pa before dividing.

exam.q: Tractors used on soft fields have very wide tyres and military tanks use caterpillar tracks. A racing car has narrow tyres. Explain, in terms of force, area and pressure, why these designs are chosen. Your answer should refer to sinking into ground and to the forces involved.
model: pressure = force / area
the weight of a tractor or tank is very large (large force on the ground)
wide tyres or tracks greatly increase the contact area
this spreads the weight so the pressure on the ground is reduced
soft ground can only withstand a limited pressure before it gives way, so low pressure stops the vehicle sinking
a racing car is light and drives on hard tarmac which can withstand high pressure, so a small contact area is acceptable and sinking is not a problem
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need a chain of reasoning: equation, force, area, pressure, consequence, comparison.

worked.q: A table of weight 240 N stands on four legs. Each leg has a square end of side 2.0 cm. Calculate the pressure on the floor in Pa.
steps: Area of one leg = 2.0 cm × 2.0 cm = 4.0 cm²

worked.q: A woman of mass 60 kg wears stiletto heels. When she rocks back, all her weight acts on one heel of area 1.0 cm². g = 10 N/kg. Compare this with an elephant of weight 40 000 N standing on four feet, each of area 0.10 m².
worked.ans: The heel exerts 6 MPa, about 60 times the elephant's 100 kPa, because its area is tiny even though the force is far smaller.

worked.q: A hydraulic jack applies a pressure of 200 000 Pa to a piston of area 0.050 m². Calculate the force produced.
steps: Recall P = F / A, rearrange to F = P × A

phy_edx.14.5.summary: The pressure in a liquid **increases with depth** and **increases with the density of the liquid**, because deeper down there is a taller, heavier column of liquid pressing from above, and a denser liquid has more mass (so more weight) in the same column. The pressure due to a column of liquid is calculated with **P = h × ρ × g** (pressure = height of column × density × gravitational field strength). Because pressure is greater at the bottom of an object than at its top, liquids push up harder than they push down, which produces an **upward force** on a submerged or partially submerged object.

core.p: The deeper you go in a liquid, the greater the pressure. At any depth, the liquid has to support the weight of all the liquid above it. Go deeper and there is a taller column of liquid above you, so more weight pushes on each square metre.
bullets: Pressure in a liquid is **directly proportional to depth** (for a given liquid and g).
Double the depth: **double the pressure due to the liquid**.
This is why dams are built **thicker at the bottom** than at the top.
Divers feel pressure on their ears increase as they swim deeper.
Submarines need thick hulls to withstand the high pressure deep in the sea.

callouts.p: Deeper means a taller column of liquid above, so a greater weight of liquid acts on each unit of area below it.

fig.cap: Water spurts from holes in a tall can. The lowest hole has the greatest depth of water above it, so the pressure there is greatest and the jet travels furthest.

core.p: At the same depth, a denser liquid exerts a greater pressure. A denser liquid packs more mass into the same volume, so the column above a point is heavier, and a heavier column pushes harder on each square metre.
bullets: Pressure is **directly proportional to density** of the liquid (same depth, same g).
Sea water (about 1030 kg/m³) gives a slightly higher pressure than fresh water (1000 kg/m³) at the same depth.
Mercury (about 13 600 kg/m³) gives about 13.6 times the pressure of water at the same depth.
Pressure also depends on **g**: the same column on the Moon would give a smaller pressure.

core.h: The equation P = h × ρ × g
core.p: The pressure due to a column of liquid depends only on the height of the column, the density of the liquid and the gravitational field strength. You must be able to recall and use it.
bullets: **pressure due to a column of liquid (Pa) = height of column (m) × density of liquid (kg/m³) × gravitational field strength (N/kg)**
Symbols: **P = h × ρ × g** (ρ is the Greek letter rho)
Rearrangements: **h = P / (ρ × g)** and **ρ = P / (h × g)**
Use **g = 10 N/kg** unless the question gives another value.
h is the **vertical depth below the surface**, not the distance along a sloping side.

callouts.p: P = h × ρ × g. Check h is in m and ρ in kg/m³ before substituting.

core.h: Where P = h × ρ × g comes from (grade 9)
core.p: You can derive it from P = F / A. Imagine a column of liquid of height h sitting on an area A. Its volume is h × A, its mass is ρ × h × A, and its weight is ρ × h × A × g. Pressure is weight divided by area, so the A cancels.
bullets: Volume of column V = h × A
Mass m = ρ × V = ρ × h × A
Weight W = m × g = ρ × h × A × g
Pressure P = W / A = **h × ρ × g**
The area cancels, which shows that **the shape or width of the container does not matter**: only depth, density and g.

callouts.p: A narrow tube and a wide tank filled to the same depth with the same liquid have the same pressure at the bottom.
