core.p: At any point in a liquid, the pressure pushes equally in all directions, and the force it produces on any surface acts at right angles (normal) to that surface. So the pressure at a given depth is the same whether a surface faces up, down or sideways.
bullets: Pressure at a point depends on **depth**, not direction.
Two points at the **same depth** in the same liquid have the **same pressure**.
The force on the side wall of a tank pushes outwards, at right angles to the wall.
Forces on the walls grow with depth, so the bottom of a tank or dam must be strongest.

core.p: The equation P = h × ρ × g gives the pressure due to the liquid only. To find the difference in pressure between two depths, use the difference in depth as h.
bullets: **ΔP = Δh × ρ × g**, where Δh is the vertical distance between the two points.
Example: points 2 m and 5 m deep in water, Δh = 3 m, ΔP = 3 × 1000 × 10 = 30 000 Pa.
This pressure difference is what causes the upward force on submerged objects.

callouts.p: Measure h from the liquid surface straight down to the point. Heights above the bottom of the tank must be subtracted from the total depth.

core.p: The air above the liquid surface also presses down, so the total pressure at a depth is atmospheric pressure plus the pressure due to the liquid. Questions usually ask only for the pressure due to the liquid, but read carefully.
bullets: **Total pressure = atmospheric pressure + h × ρ × g**
Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about **100 000 Pa**.
In water, every 10 m of depth adds about 100 000 Pa (10 × 1000 × 10), roughly one extra atmosphere.
So at 10 m deep in water the total pressure is about 200 000 Pa.

callouts.p: 'Pressure due to the water' means h × ρ × g only. 'Total pressure' means add atmospheric pressure too.

core.h: Why this produces an upward force
core.p: For an object in a liquid, its bottom surface is deeper than its top surface. The pressure at the bottom is therefore greater than at the top. The liquid pushes up on the bottom with a bigger force than it pushes down on the top, so there is a resultant upward force on the object.
bullets: Pressure on the **bottom face > pressure on the top face** (bottom is deeper).
Force = pressure × area, so the **upward force on the bottom > downward force on the top**.
The sideways forces on the vertical sides cancel out, because at each depth they are equal and opposite.
Result: a **net upward force** on the object (this is upthrust, covered in the next spec point).
For a partially submerged object, only the bottom is in the liquid, so the liquid pushes up on it and there is no liquid pushing down on the top.

callouts.p: Bottom deeper, so greater pressure, so greater force upwards than downwards, so resultant upward force.

core.p: Many everyday and engineering designs are explained by pressure increasing with depth and density.
bullets: **Dams**: wider at the base to withstand the greater water pressure at depth.
**Submarines and deep-sea submersibles**: thick, strong hulls; deep-sea fish have bodies adapted to high pressure.
**Water towers**: placed high up so the large depth of water gives high pressure in taps below.
**Divers**: must equalise pressure in their ears; pressure increases by about 1 atmosphere every 10 m.
**Drips and blood pressure**: an IV bag is hung higher to give more pressure to push fluid into a vein.

core.p: Lay out every liquid pressure calculation in the same way so you collect all the method marks.
bullets: 1. Write the equation: **P = h × ρ × g**.
2. Convert: cm to m (divide by 100), g/cm³ to kg/m³ (multiply by 1000), kPa to Pa.
3. Rearrange if you need h or ρ.
4. Substitute numbers and calculate.
5. Give the unit (Pa) and decide whether atmospheric pressure needs adding.

callouts.p: Water is 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. Using 1 instead of 1000 makes the answer 1000 times too small.

core.p: Because P is proportional to both h and ρ, you can compare situations using ratios without full calculation.
bullets: Same pressure in two liquids needs **h × ρ equal**: oil (800 kg/m³) needs 1.25 times the depth of water to give the same pressure.
Doubling depth and halving density gives the **same pressure**.
A graph of liquid pressure against depth is a **straight line through the origin**; a denser liquid gives a **steeper line**.
If total pressure (including the atmosphere) is plotted, the line does not pass through the origin; it starts at atmospheric pressure.

analogy.p: Think of a liquid as a pile of books stacked on your hand. The book at the bottom of the pile supports every book above it, so it is squashed the most, just like liquid at the bottom of a tank. Swap paperbacks for heavy encyclopaedias (a denser liquid) and the same height of stack presses much harder. It breaks down because books only push down, while liquid pressure pushes equally in all directions, including sideways and upwards; and a liquid flows to fill its container rather than staying as a separate stack.

terms.d: Force normal to a surface per unit area of that surface; unit Pa.
A substance that can flow: a liquid or a gas.
Vertical distance below the surface of the liquid, in metres.
Mass per unit volume, ρ = m / V, measured in kg/m³.
Force per unit mass due to gravity; 10 N/kg on Earth.
The vertical body of liquid directly above a point, whose weight causes the pressure there.
P = h × ρ × g; the pressure caused by the weight of the liquid only.
Pressure caused by the weight of air above; about 100 000 Pa at sea level.
Atmospheric pressure plus the pressure due to the liquid.
Difference between pressures at two depths; ΔP = Δh × ρ × g.
At right angles to a surface; forces from fluid pressure act normal to surfaces.
Doubling one quantity doubles the other; liquid pressure is directly proportional to depth and to density.
The resultant upward force exerted by a fluid on an object in it, caused by greater pressure at greater depth.
Unit of pressure, equal to 1 N/m².

mistakes.w: Pressure is greater at the bottom because the water is heavier there.
mistakes.r: There is a greater depth (taller column) of water above, so a greater weight of water acts on each unit area.

mistakes.w: A wider container has a greater pressure at the bottom.
mistakes.r: Pressure depends only on depth, density and g; the area cancels out.

mistakes.w: Using density of water as 1 in P = h × ρ × g.
mistakes.r: Use 1000 kg/m³.

mistakes.w: Using depth in cm.
mistakes.r: Convert to metres first.

mistakes.w: Liquid pressure only acts downwards.
mistakes.r: Pressure at a point acts in all directions; the force on any surface is normal to it.

mistakes.w: Measuring h from the bottom of the tank.
mistakes.r: h is measured from the surface down to the point.

mistakes.w: Objects get an upward force because water is pushing them up from underneath only.
mistakes.r: Pressure is greater on the deeper bottom surface than the top surface, so the upward force exceeds the downward force.

mistakes.w: Writing P = h × ρ / g.
mistakes.r: P = h × ρ × g.

exam.q: Describe how the pressure in a liquid changes as depth increases.
model: pressure increases (in proportion to depth)
exam.tip: 'Increases' is enough for 1 mark; 'proportionally' shows extra understanding.

exam.q: State the equation linking pressure due to a column of liquid, height of the column, density of the liquid and gravitational field strength.
model: pressure = height of column × density of liquid × gravitational field strength (P = h × ρ × g)
exam.tip: Use the spec words 'height of column'.

exam.q: Calculate the pressure due to water at a depth of 4.0 m. Density of water = 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 N/kg.
exam.tip: Remember the unit.

exam.q: Explain why a dam is thicker at the bottom than at the top.
model: pressure in the water increases with depth
so a greater force acts on the bottom of the dam, which must be stronger
exam.tip: Mention depth and pressure, then force.

exam.q: A diver is at 25 m depth in sea water of density 1030 kg/m³. g = 10 N/kg. Calculate the pressure due to the water.
model: P = 257 500 Pa (accept 258 000 Pa)
exam.tip: Check powers of ten carefully.

exam.q: A pressure of 12 000 Pa is measured at a depth of 1.5 m in an oil. g = 10 N/kg. Calculate the density of the oil.
model: ρ = P / (h × g)
ρ = 800 kg/m³
exam.tip: Rearrange first, then substitute.

exam.q: Two tanks contain the same liquid to the same depth. Tank A is narrow and tank B is wide. Compare the pressure at the bottom of each tank and explain your answer.
model: the pressure is the same
because pressure depends only on depth, density and g, not on area or shape
exam.tip: A common trap; do not say the wide tank has more pressure.

exam.q: Explain why the pressure at a given depth in sea water is greater than at the same depth in fresh water.
model: sea water is denser (more mass per unit volume)
so the column of liquid above has a greater weight, giving greater pressure (P = h × ρ × g)
exam.tip: Link density to weight of the column.

exam.q: A swimming pool is 2.0 m deep. Atmospheric pressure is 100 000 Pa. Calculate the total pressure at the bottom. Density of water = 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 N/kg.
model: pressure due to water = 2.0 × 1000 × 10 = 20 000 Pa
total = 120 000 Pa
exam.tip: 'Total' signals that atmospheric pressure is added.

exam.q: A block is held fully under water. Explain, in terms of pressure, why the water exerts a resultant upward force on the block.
model: the bottom surface of the block is deeper than the top surface
pressure increases with depth so the pressure on the bottom is greater
force = pressure × area, so the upward force on the bottom is greater than the downward force on the top
forces on the sides cancel, so there is a resultant upward force
exam.tip: Build a chain of reasoning from depth to pressure to force.

exam.q: Explain how the pressure in a liquid depends on depth and density, and why. Include the equation and how it can be derived from pressure = force / area.
model: pressure increases with depth and with density
at a point, the liquid supports the weight of the column of liquid above it
deeper means a taller column, so more weight per unit area
denser liquid means more mass in the column, so more weight per unit area
weight of column = h × A × ρ × g, and P = weight / A
so P = h × ρ × g; area cancels so shape of container does not matter
exam.tip: Organise into: what happens, why, equation, derivation, consequence.

worked.q: A submarine window is at a depth of 200 m in sea water (density 1030 kg/m³, g = 10 N/kg). The window has an area of 0.050 m². Calculate the pressure due to the water and the force on the window.
worked.ans: Pressure = 2 060 000 Pa (about 2.1 MPa); force on window = 103 000 N

worked.q: A tank holds water 80 cm deep. Calculate the difference in pressure between a point 20 cm below the surface and the bottom of the tank. Density 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 N/kg.
steps: Depth of bottom = 0.80 m, depth of point = 0.20 m

worked.q: At what depth in oil (density 800 kg/m³) is the pressure due to the oil equal to 20 000 Pa? g = 10 N/kg.

phy_edx.14.6.summary: Any object partly or fully in a fluid feels an upward force called **upthrust**, because the fluid pressure on its deeper bottom surface is greater than on its top surface. The size of the upthrust is **equal to the weight of fluid displaced** by the object. An object **floats** when it can displace a weight of fluid equal to its own weight before it is fully submerged (so its density is less than the fluid's), and it **sinks** when even fully submerged the upthrust is less than its weight (its density is greater than the fluid's).

core.p: Upthrust is the resultant upward force a fluid (liquid or gas) exerts on an object that is partly or completely immersed in it. It is caused by the pressure in a fluid increasing with depth.
bullets: Upthrust acts **vertically upwards** on the object.
It acts in **liquids and gases** (e.g. a helium balloon in air feels upthrust).
It exists whether the object floats or sinks: a sinking stone still feels upthrust, just not enough to support it.
Measured in **newtons (N)**, because it is a force.

callouts.p: The upward force exerted by a fluid on an object immersed (partly or fully) in it; it is equal to the weight of fluid displaced.

core.p: Pressure in a fluid increases with depth. The bottom of an immersed object is deeper than its top, so the fluid pushes up on the bottom harder than it pushes down on the top. The sideways forces on the sides balance. The result is a net upward force.
bullets: Pressure at bottom face **>** pressure at top face (bottom is deeper).
Force = pressure × area, so **upward force on bottom > downward force on top**.
Horizontal forces on the sides are equal and opposite at each depth, so they cancel.
Resultant: **upthrust upwards**.
For a floating object only the bottom is in the liquid, so there is pressure pushing up but none from the liquid pushing down.

callouts.p: Deeper bottom → greater pressure → greater upward force → resultant upward force (upthrust).

core.h: Upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced
core.p: When an object is put into a fluid it pushes some fluid out of the way. This is the displaced fluid. The upthrust on the object is exactly equal to the weight of this displaced fluid. This is often called Archimedes' principle.
bullets: **Upthrust = weight of fluid displaced**.
Volume of fluid displaced = **volume of the part of the object that is submerged**.
Weight of fluid displaced = **density of fluid × volume displaced × g**.
So **upthrust = ρ(fluid) × V(submerged) × g**.
The deeper an object is pushed in (until fully submerged), the more fluid it displaces and the bigger the upthrust.
Once fully submerged, pushing it deeper does **not** increase upthrust (the volume displaced stays the same).

callouts.p: Imagine the object replaced by fluid of the same shape. That fluid would be in equilibrium, so the surrounding pressure forces on it (the upthrust) must equal its weight. The object feels exactly the same surrounding pressure forces.

fig.cap: Lowering a block into a full displacement can: the water pushed out is collected. The newton-meter reading drops by the weight of the water displaced, which equals the upthrust.

core.p: An object floats when the upthrust on it equals its weight. A floating object sinks into the fluid just far enough to displace a weight of fluid equal to its own weight, and then the forces are balanced.
bullets: Floating: **upthrust = weight**, so the resultant force is zero (object in equilibrium).
The object settles at the depth where **weight of fluid displaced = weight of object**.
A heavier load makes a boat sit lower in the water so it displaces more water.
A floating object is only partly submerged if its average density is less than the fluid's.

callouts.p: An object floats if it can displace its own weight of fluid before it becomes fully submerged.

core.p: An object sinks when its weight is greater than the maximum upthrust it can get. The maximum upthrust happens when the object is fully submerged, because then it displaces the most fluid it can (its own volume).
bullets: Sinking: **weight > upthrust** even when fully submerged.
Resultant force is **downwards**, so the object accelerates down (until drag or the bottom stops it).
A solid steel ball sinks because the water it displaces weighs much less than the ball.
On the bottom, the floor supplies the extra upward (reaction) force needed for balance.

core.p: Whether an object floats or sinks depends on how its density compares with the density of the fluid. If it is less dense, a submerged volume smaller than its whole volume is enough to displace its own weight of fluid.
bullets: **Object less dense than fluid → floats.**
**Object more dense than fluid → sinks.**
Object with the **same density** as the fluid → stays at whatever depth it is placed (neutral buoyancy).
Water density is 1000 kg/m³: wood (about 600 kg/m³) floats, steel (about 7800 kg/m³) sinks.
For a floating object, **fraction submerged = density of object / density of fluid** (e.g. ice at 920 kg/m³ floats about 92% under water).

callouts.t: Weight is not the deciding factor
callouts.p: A huge log floats and a tiny pebble sinks. It is density (or weight compared with upthrust), not weight alone, that decides.

core.p: Steel is much denser than water, yet ships float. The hull is shaped so that it encloses a large volume of air. The ship's average density (steel plus air inside) is less than water, and the large hull displaces a very large volume of water.
bullets: Shaping steel into a hollow hull **increases the volume** of water that can be displaced.
The weight of water displaced can then equal the ship's weight before the hull is fully submerged.
The **average density** of the ship (total mass / total volume including air) is less than water.
Overloading lowers the ship until it can no longer displace enough water and it sinks.
**Plimsoll lines** on ships show safe loading depths; a ship floats lower in less dense fresh water than in sea water.

callouts.p: Fresh water is less dense, so a ship must displace a larger volume of it to make the same upthrust; it therefore sits lower in fresh water.

core.h: Factors that influence floating and sinking
core.p: Several factors combine to decide whether an object floats or sinks and how deep it sits.
bullets: **Weight (mass) of the object**: more weight needs more upthrust.
**Volume and shape of the object**: a larger volume can displace more fluid, giving more possible upthrust.
**Average density of the object** compared with the fluid.
**Density of the fluid**: denser fluid gives more upthrust for the same volume displaced (it is easier to float in the Dead Sea).
**Gravitational field strength** affects both weight and upthrust equally, so it does not change whether an object floats.

core.p: A submarine changes its average density to rise, sink or stay at a set depth, using ballast tanks.
bullets: To **dive**: ballast tanks are flooded with sea water, weight increases, weight > upthrust.
To **surface**: compressed air pushes water out of the tanks, weight decreases, upthrust > weight.
To **hover**: water is adjusted until weight = upthrust when fully submerged.
Fish use a gas-filled **swim bladder** in a similar way; hot-air balloons rise because the hot air inside is less dense than the surrounding air.

core.p: When an object hanging from a newton-meter is lowered into a liquid, the reading falls. The upthrust supports part of its weight.
bullets: **Apparent weight = true weight - upthrust**.
So **upthrust = weight in air - reading in liquid**.
The reading falls as more of the object is submerged, then stays constant once it is fully submerged.
This is why objects feel lighter when lifted under water.

callouts.p: Subtract the reading in water from the reading in air. Example: 8.0 N in air, 5.0 N in water, upthrust = 3.0 N.

core.p: Air is a fluid too, so every object in air feels a small upthrust equal to the weight of air it displaces. Because air is about 1.2 kg/m³, this is normally tiny compared with an object's weight.
bullets: A helium balloon rises because the weight of air it displaces is greater than its total weight (balloon plus helium).
A hot-air balloon rises when heated air inside makes its average density less than the cooler surrounding air.
Upthrust in air decreases with height because air density decreases.

analogy.p: Imagine a tightly packed crowd of people (the fluid). When you push into the crowd, the people you shove aside push back on you with the same total effort they used to hold up the people who used to stand there. If you are lighter than the people you pushed aside, they lift you up (you float); if you are heavier, they cannot hold you (you sink). It breaks down because fluid pressure is caused by depth and acts at right angles to every surface, and real fluid does not 'decide' to push; it is the pressure difference between top and bottom that produces the force.

terms.d: The upward force exerted by a fluid on an object partly or fully immersed in it.
A liquid or a gas; a substance that can flow.
Fluid pushed out of the way by an object placed in it; its volume equals the submerged volume.
The upthrust on an object equals the weight of fluid it displaces.

mistakes.w: Objects float because they are light.
mistakes.r: Objects float if their density is less than the fluid's, so upthrust can equal weight before they are fully submerged.

mistakes.w: Sinking objects have no upthrust.
mistakes.r: All immersed objects have upthrust; for a sinking object it is less than its weight.

mistakes.w: Upthrust equals the weight of the object.
mistakes.r: Upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced; this equals the object's weight only when it floats or hovers.

mistakes.w: Upthrust keeps increasing as an object goes deeper.
mistakes.r: Once fully submerged the volume displaced is constant, so upthrust stays the same.

mistakes.w: Upthrust is caused by water pushing up from underneath.
mistakes.r: Pressure increases with depth, so pressure on the bottom surface is greater than on the top, giving a resultant upward force.

mistakes.w: A steel ship floats because steel is light.
mistakes.r: The hollow hull gives a large volume (lots of air), so the average density is less than water and it displaces its own weight of water.

mistakes.w: Upthrust = volume of water displaced.
mistakes.r: Upthrust = weight of fluid displaced (a force in N), found from ρ × V × g.

mistakes.w: Ships float higher in fresh water.
mistakes.r: Fresh water is less dense, so a greater volume must be displaced; ships float lower in fresh water.

exam.q: State what is meant by upthrust.
model: the upward force exerted by a fluid on an object (partly or fully) immersed in it
exam.tip: Say 'upward force' and 'fluid'.

exam.q: State how the size of the upthrust on an object is related to the fluid it displaces.
model: upthrust is equal to the weight of fluid displaced
exam.tip: 'Weight', not 'volume'.

exam.q: A stone weighs 6.0 N in air and 3.8 N when fully immersed in water. Calculate the upthrust.
model: upthrust = 6.0 - 3.8
exam.tip: Upthrust is the drop in reading.

exam.q: Explain why a piece of wood floats in water but a piece of iron of the same size sinks.
model: both displace the same volume and weight of water so have the same maximum upthrust
wood is less dense than water so its weight is less than the maximum upthrust; it floats with upthrust = weight
iron is denser than water so its weight is greater than the upthrust and it sinks
exam.tip: Compare weight with upthrust, or density with water's density.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of pressure, why there is an upthrust on an object immersed in a liquid.
model: pressure in a liquid increases with depth
the bottom of the object is deeper so has a greater pressure (and force) on it than the top
giving a resultant upward force
exam.tip: Mention depth, then pressure, then force.

exam.q: A block of volume 0.020 m³ is fully submerged in water of density 1000 kg/m³. g = 10 N/kg. Calculate the upthrust on it.
model: mass of water displaced = 1000 × 0.020 = 20 kg
weight of water displaced = 20 × 10
upthrust = 200 N
exam.tip: Volume displaced equals the submerged volume.

exam.q: A boat of weight 15 000 N floats on a lake. State the upthrust on the boat and the weight of water it displaces.
model: upthrust = 15 000 N
weight of water displaced = 15 000 N
exam.tip: Floating means upthrust equals weight.

exam.q: Explain why a ship sits lower in fresh water than in sea water.
model: the upthrust must still equal the ship's weight
fresh water is less dense than sea water
so a greater volume of fresh water must be displaced to give the same weight, so the ship sinks lower
exam.tip: Keep the weight constant in your reasoning.

exam.q: Describe how a submarine is able to dive and then return to the surface.
model: to dive, ballast tanks are filled with water
this increases its weight (average density) so weight > upthrust and it sinks
to surface, compressed air forces water out of the tanks
weight decreases so upthrust > weight and it rises
exam.tip: Always compare weight with upthrust in each stage.

exam.q: Steel is about eight times as dense as water, yet large steel ships float. Explain how this is possible and describe what happens as more cargo is loaded. Refer to upthrust, weight, volume and density.
model: a solid block of steel sinks because its weight is greater than the weight of water it displaces
a ship's hull is hollow and encloses a large volume of air
so it can displace a large volume (and weight) of water
the average density of the ship is less than that of water
it floats where upthrust (weight of water displaced) equals its weight
adding cargo increases weight so the ship sits lower, displacing more water, until if overloaded it cannot displace enough water and sinks
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need a linked sequence; use 'weight of water displaced' explicitly.

worked.q: An ice cube of volume 40 cm³ and density 920 kg/m³ floats in water (1000 kg/m³). g = 10 N/kg. Calculate its weight and the volume of it that is submerged.
steps: Floating: upthrust = 0.368 N = weight of water displaced
Mass of water displaced = 0.0368 kg, volume = 0.0368 / 1000 = 0.0000368 m³
worked.ans: Weight 0.368 N; submerged volume 36.8 cm³

worked.q: A metal object weighs 12.0 N in air. When fully immersed in water its newton-meter reading is 8.0 N. Calculate the upthrust, the volume of the object and its density. Water density 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 N/kg.
steps: Weight of water displaced = 4.0 N, so mass displaced = 4.0 / 10 = 0.40 kg
Volume displaced = 0.40 / 1000 = 0.00040 m³ = volume of object
worked.ans: Upthrust 4.0 N; volume 0.00040 m³; density 3000 kg/m³ (so it sinks)
